articles.title: Heat-related deaths up 36% since Paris Agreement as climate action lags: Lancet
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Some of the health harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement entered into force (2016-2025) than in the previous decade (2006-2015) as climate action fails to keep pace, according to the 10th Lancet Countdown Report on Health and Climate Change .
The report, which was released on Wednesday, said the annual average heat-related deaths rose by nearly 36% globally after the Paris Agreement was introduced.
"In 2023 alone, heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths with more than 70 per cent of that toll attributable to human-caused climate change," it said.

The analysis represents the work of 146 multidisciplinary researchers from more than 100 institutions across more than 30 countries. It tracks 54 indicators of the health impacts of climate change and the health effects of climate action.

The report highlights that cleaner energy, more resilient health systems, more health-protecting legislation and growing scientific evidence have brought real health benefits to local communities since the Paris Agreement, but these gains are still too slow, too insufficient, and too inconsistent to offset the growing risks.
"Rising overall energy demand and slow system change means fossil fuels still supply over 80% of the world's energy, and climate-heating emissions reached a record high in 2024," it said.
The report added that despite gains in some countries, fossil-fuel air pollution still kills an estimated 2.8 million people a year worldwide.
Moreover, adaptation funding is falling far short of what's needed.

According to the report, the health adaptation needs quantified so far by developing countries put the minimum cost at $3.3 billion a year, based on data from only 48 of the 79 countries that have completed these estimates.
However, only around a third of this declared need, $1.1 billion, was committed in 2024.

"This substantial financing gap is reflected in countries' ability to translate adaptation priorities into action, with finance and human resourcing identified as the top barriers to implementation of Health National Adaptation Plans," said the report.

articles.title: Why ongoing symptoms and patients’ lived experiences need more attention in lupus care
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: When Nisha Panwar,30, was diagnosed with lupus in December 2013, she felt relieved. After months of recurrent fever, rashes and worsening symptoms, she finally had an explanation for what was happening to her body. Before the diagnosis, she says, several doctors had told her she had no disease and that it was “all in my head” and was referred to a psychiatrist.

For Tabassum Sultana, 28, a Bengaluru-based content creator, the diagnosis of mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), with features of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), in 2024 was followed by another setback. She developed avascular necrosis of the right hip and underwent surgery in September 2025. Her recovery was slow, she became dependent on her mother for everyday activities and had to stop working. Recurring flare-ups continue to affect her mental health.

articles.title: Hunker down: On Cyclone Arnab, its landfall
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Cyclone Arnab, the first named storm of the North Indian Ocean cyclone season this year, intensified rapidly before making landfall as a ‘very severe cyclonic storm’ on October 28. This particular rapidity is a challenge for forecasters and some models did fail to anticipate how strong Arnab would become. It also moved faster than expected towards the coast, before stalling for a time and beginning the landfall process several hours before the India Meteorological Department (IMD) had predicted it would, in the middle of the night, leaving many district authorities with a potentially narrower window to evacuate high-risk settlements. With core wind speeds of 125-135 kilometres per hour, it delivered more than 100 mm of rain over parts of Anakapalli, Visakhapatnam, Kalingapatnam, Kakinada and Machilipatnam, in Andhra Pradesh. But even though it has completed landfall, southern Odisha likely faces a greater threat only hence. Early reports claimed no loss of life in Andhra Pradesh or Odisha, which has been attributed to the disaster management operations in both States; the Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister, N. Chandrababu Naidu, said there were five deaths in Andhra Pradesh . Regrettably, the suspension of transport services, including road connectivity and flights, closure of schools and offices, and power cuts to minimise risks posed by loose wires remains an essential part of saving lives, entailing other social and economic disruptions that the States must account for, and address, in their post-storm assessments.

Odisha may have to brace for rainfall and waters due to moisture in the storm’s outer circulation, which will arrive over land that has recovered in patches from the fourth wettest monsoon in the State’s history. Extreme rainfall after repeated flooding may face soil that has not drained fully, raising the risk of more flooding following even lower levels of rainfall, and slope failures in hilly terrain. Farmers in Ganjam and Puri have already voiced worries about the risk of prolonged inundation destroying paddy crops, compounding the already considerable financial consequences of the southwest monsoon; Ganjam alone had lost 33% of crops by October. In Sundargarh, however, farmers hope that Arnab will relieve moisture stress in standing crops after a dry month. The IMD has already issued alerts in the Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput, Malkangiri, Nabarangpur, and Kalahandi districts, before the rainbelt extends further north. The relatively low figure of deaths will be a testament to proactive governance. However, it is past time that States adopted a zero-disruption approach, especially since property and infrastructure were damaged, and the risk of people being pushed into poverty over lost possessions and livelihoods persists.

articles.title: Clinging on: On Netanyahu and the Israel elections
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Benjamin Netanyahu was at the centre of Israel’s October 27 elections. For Israel’s longest-serving Prime Minister, who oversaw a genocidal war in Gaza following Hamas’s October 7 attack , the election was the biggest test of his political career. For the Opposition, which promised to hold him accountable for the failures of October 7 and end the country’s “forever wars”, the election offered an opportunity to oust him from power. The results, however, sent a mixed message. With 85.6% of the votes counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition has lost its majority but is still the largest bloc . His Likud party is projected to win 26 seats, while its main rival Yashar, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is expected to secure 21. Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, the far-right extremist parties in Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition, demonstrated their continued strength, winning 13 seats between them. The dark horse, however, could be the Arab parties — the Joint List is projected to win 12 seats while the United Arab List (Ra’am) could secure seven seats. With neither bloc commanding a majority, the Arab parties could propel the opposition coalition to power. But the big question is whether the anti-Netanyahu coalition is ready to join hands with the Arab parties, which have historically been kept on the margins of Israel’ s power politics.

Mr. Netanyahu’s central promise has been that only he can guarantee Israel’s security. Yet, the October 7 attack took place on his watch and he has refused to take responsibility for the failures that led to it. A wanted man by the International Criminal Court, he has repeated, before and after October 7, that a Palestine state would not be formed while he is in power. His war on Gaza has killed over 70,000 Palestinians, including 20,000 children, and displaced the region’s population. Israel’s brutal occupation machinery has also expanded and tightened its control of the West Bank, while settler terrorists have unleashed violence on Palestinian households. His war on Iran has been a disaster, with global economic consequences. Mr. Netanyahu has sought to portray his wars as bold, necessary moves to protect Israel, while exploiting Israelis’ security concerns for political gain. He may not be voted out immediately, but his failure to secure a majority and the decline in his party’s popularity are significant. The Opposition should take its cue from the results and form a broad coalition with the Arab parties. It should restore accountability in governance, revisit his unchecked militarism and rebuild ties with the world. If Mr. Netanyahu continues to cling to power, it would be bad news for Israel and the region.

articles.title: Small fish: On Operation Trident
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Operation Trident , a multi-agency crackdown on an international syndicate operating across the India-Myanmar-Bangladesh corridor, marks a significant step-up in the government’s campaign against drug trafficking. The Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has set December 31, 2029, as the deadline to eradicate drug networks across the country. The October 23 raids, which led to 18 people being arrested , were based on NCB investigations following the arrest of an alleged Myanmar-based kingpin in Delhi this May. However, the dismantling of the entire network would require identification of all suppliers in Myanmar and their successful prosecution. The government’s strategy, involving States and Union Territories, over 40 Ministries, central agencies and the pharmaceutical sector, is outlined in the Vision Document on Drug Control (2026-2029), launched by Mr. Shah at the Narco-Coordination Centre meeting on June 26, 2026. It envisages dismantling 100 major cartels and improving prosecution outcomes. The broad strategy reflects the complexity of the problem and signals a more focused approach. Data for 2025 also show an increase of over 50% in arrests and a nearly 53% rise in cases registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act compared with 2024.

However, the government’s action-plan will depend on consistent implementation and efficient coordination among agencies, and striking at the real brains behind it all. In several cases, foreign-based key operatives still remain at large and big sharks often do not fall in the net. The 2021 Mundra port case in Gujarat, involving the seizure of about 3,000 kg of heroin, is a case in point wherein the principal Afghanistan-based suppliers have yet to be brought to book. Also, the quantity of drugs seized does not, by itself, indicate whether drug availability or consumption has declined. Punjab remains a prominent example of the continuing public health challenges associated with drug abuse. The alleged drug-related killings of anti-drug activists in Mansa and Gurdaspur, along with the alleged death by suicide of a father in Sangrur who had raised concerns about the easy availability of synthetic drugs in his locality, underscore the human cost of the problem. These incidents also raise questions about the protection of those who speak out against drug trafficking and networks. These concerns lend urgency to the objective of dismantling entire networks and apprehending the “big sharks”, rather than concentrating disproportionately on individual carriers. The key is to identify the ultimate beneficiaries by meticulously following the money trail and ensuring their conviction.

articles.title: Fouled waters: On Rajasthan’s river pollution
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Supreme Court has pulled up, once again, the Rajasthan government over industrial effluents flowing into the Jojari river and the deadly risk it poses for the people depending on it. The problem is decades old — public interest litigation in the Rajasthan High Court alerted State machinery to the problem in 2011 — indicating an oversight by the State bordering on the systematic. The Jojari, the Luni, and the Bandi are seasonal rivers in the State’s arid western region, flowing through Jodhpur, Balotra, and Pali districts. This region has also evolved as a textile-dyeing and steelworking hub, and untreated or insufficiently treated effluents from these factories have run directly into the rivers and soil, endangering the health of around 20 lakh local residents. The region also suffers rampant illegal sand mining in riverbeds. The sewage treatment plants have been able to accommodate only around half of the sewage generated in the three urban centres, according to the State’s submissions to the Court in 2025, even as the Court recorded substantial underutilisation at common effluent treatment plants. The combination is suggestive of industrial sources bypassing treatment facilities, poor connections between the sources and the facilities, and/or insufficient capacity at particular sites or in specific periods.

The Court initiated a suo motu writ petition in 2025 and constituted a High-level Ecosystem Oversight Committee chaired by Justice Sangeet Lodha to audit the plants and draft a plan to restore the rivers. Based on the committee’s scathing status reports, Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta banned construction within 100 metres of the rivers’ edges and hazardous industries within 500 m of the present path, or of the flood lines where available. The Court has also upbraided local authorities for failing to enforce pollution norms by citing the Court’s own stay of a 2022 National Green Tribunal order imposing a compensation on the Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation and the local administration in Jodhpur and Barmer. The State regulatory apparatus has been dysfunctional: officials were aware of illegal mining operations in some areas, yet they regularised leases in those areas. Given the dereliction in play, the Court is correct to treat the possibility of collusion between State officials and industrial mafias seriously. Justice Mehta’s observation that the State could be held liable under the ‘polluter pays’ principle is also a significant indictment of state failure, through negligence. Now, importantly, the State still has to restore the Jojari and attend to its wellbeing, which is relevant to a recent tendency by the Court to substitute itself for regulators rather than disciplining them into discharging their functions. This needs to change.

articles.title: Dubious retreat: On the National Medical Commission and its MSMER
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has denotified and withdrawn its 2023 Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations (MSMER ), diminishing the framework of penalties vis-à-vis educational standards and infrastructure at medical colleges. The move is noteworthy as the MSMER provided for fines of up to ₹5 lakh on faculty members and administrators for submitting false information. Fortunately, the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) retains the power to fine errant institutions up to ₹1 crore under the 2023 Establishment of Medical Institutions, Assessment and Rating Regulations . MSMER was lauded for its intention to crack down on the deep-seated corruption and malpractice in medical colleges, particularly over ‘ghost faculty’ and ‘ghost patients’. The NMC’s justification is that MSMER also introduced a parallel mechanism allowing undergraduate and postgraduate boards to evaluate institutions, stepping on the MARB’s toes. However, why the NMC scrapped MSMER wholesale is unclear. The 2023 Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations remain in force and include a provision to fine individual faculty members at postgraduate medical colleges. Non-compliance among medical colleges is not uncommon and seldom nipped in the bud, even as the number of medical seats swells while the transparency of the medical education system has not improved.

Notwithstanding the provision to fine individuals at postgraduate centres, the MARB and the NMC can only penalise institutions, which is harder and risks creating a perverse incentive to accommodate rather than punish, and could mitigate the fear that keeps administrators honest. MSMER also specified timelines to appeal penalties. Although the MARB regulations retain the appeal processes, their 15-day deadline could conflict with the 60-day period under the NMC Act, potentially creating legal disputes that delay penal action. There is also a telling incident. As part of a proceeding under the RTI Act, the Central Information Commission revealed last year that the NMC had stated in 2024 that MARB had neither formally assessed nor rated medical colleges and that its standard forms need not be made public. In a revised reply in October 2025, it said the responding NMC officer’s records did not include any of the corresponding reports. However, the 2023 MARB regulations require the Board to publish its latest annual assessment results. If the NMC withdrew MSMER because the powers thereunder also exist elsewhere, the public deserves to know whether the powers are also being exercised and whether the outcomes are as publicly accessible as intended. Unless the NMC has satisfactory answers for all these lacunae, the withdrawal will appear less like simplification and more like regulatory relaxation.

articles.title: A final surge: On Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s triumph in Brazil
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: At one point, it seemed almost impossible for Brazil’s 80-year-old President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, to turn the tide after finishing second to Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of elections on October 4. In Brazil’s history, no candidate who has finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidential run-off. Most of the candidates who dropped out after the first round were from the right. Flávio’s Liberal Party cemented its position in both houses of Congress, while right-wing candidates won several provincial elections. But Lula, a former trade unionist and organiser, who lost a finger in an accident as a teenager, was not ready to give up. Lula and his Workers’ Party identified campaign weaknesses, shifted their attention to economic issues, promised growth and welfare, and persuaded more voters to turn out for Sunday’s run-off. Lula won 51.7% of the vote against Flávio’s 48.2%, a greater lead than his victory against Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, four years ago. Over the weeks, Lula turned the right-wing’s gains in the first round against it, highlighting the threats that a Bolsonaro victory could pose to democracy and civil rights. Flávio’s campaign pledge to free his father — he is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn Lula’s 2022 victory, and impeach Supreme Court judges — only heightened the concerns of voters outside the right wing, who rallied behind a familiar face.

Lula unleashed a social media campaign to mobilise younger voters. A WhatsApp channel called ‘Lula’s Army’ with 11 million followers spread his message of continuity. He also announced plans to expand a cash payout scheme for the poor, a new debt relief package and entrepreneur-friendly measures. In the northeast, the Workers’ Party’s stronghold, he gained nearly three million votes and made considerable gains in the working-class neighbourhoods of big cities, including São Paulo. A relatively stable economic record, marked by growth and falling unemployment over the past three and a half years, also lent credibility to Lula’s appeal. His victory bucks the recent trend in South America, where Washington-aligned right-wing and conservative forces have gained ground. While Lula offers predictable stability and social and economic inclusiveness, he could also be, as the President of South America’s largest economy, a voice of resistance to Donald Trump’s imperial ambitions. At the same time, Lula will have to work with a right-wing-controlled Congress to advance his agenda. He should seek to build legislative consensus while focusing on addressing the economic challenges of Brazil, which remains one of the most unequal major world economies.

articles.title: Open to investigation: on the challenge to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Digital News Publishers Association’s (DNPA) challenge to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and its Rules, has drawn attention to concerns that a law to safeguard informational privacy risks creating a serious chilling effect on the media. The absence of a specific exemption for journalistic activity could subject reporters investigating official misconduct or corruption to the obligations of a “data fiduciary”, requiring them to notify and seek consent from the very individuals they are investigating. Such onerous requirements could affect investigations undertaken in the public interest. The implications extend to routine newsgathering too, where personal information is integral to reporting. The omission is particularly consequential because the drafts in 2018, 2019 and 2021 carried a journalistic exemption. The Act already provides exemptions for certain forms of data processing, including for research and statistical purposes, making the denial of similar protection to journalists difficult to justify. Non-compliance can attract penalties of up to ₹250 crore, posing an existential threat to smaller and independent newsrooms. The DNPA petition also challenges Section 44(3), which amended the RTI Act, 2005, removing the earlier public-interest qualification concerning disclosure of personal information. The protection of personal information must not be absolute; an overriding public interest must remain a legitimate ground for disclosure, particularly when the information is held by public authorities. Investigations into corruption often rely on asset disclosures and tender documents containing personal data. Restricting access to these records risks reducing journalism to merely reproducing government releases.

The Supreme Court, while issuing notice on the petition, rightly emphasised the need to balance press freedom with the right to privacy. Although journalists in India enjoy no specific statutory protection for their work, freedom of the press is constitutionally protected under Article 19(1)(a). The Court has also shielded newspapers from arbitrary state restrictions. However, growing mistrust of legacy media and the rise of independent content creators have made it difficult to determine who receives such protection. The Centre has also flagged this concern. Yet, carving out distinct categories is no easy task — a 2026 Reuters Institute report shows that the proportion of 18- to 24-year-olds identifying social media as their primary source of news rose from 21% in 2015 to 39% in 2025. A purely legalistic determination of these competing concerns may perhaps prove too onerous. Stakeholders must build consensus on a mutually acceptable framework where public functionaries and those handling public funds are not insulated from scrutiny under the guise of privacy. Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw’s indication that he would meet editors is a welcome step towards consensus.

articles.title: Deemed ineligible: on the Supreme Court and SIR
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: At Wednesday’s hearing of a petition on the Delhi SIR in the Supreme Court, Justice Joymalya Bagchi asked questions that cut to the heart of the Election Commission of India (ECI)’s SIR of electoral rolls. If an existing voter was “lax, inert or did not respond” to enumeration forms, was that a ground for the ECI to “forfeit his or her right to vote forever”? The Bench headed by the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said that the ECI was in “error” to force such voters, struck off for not returning enumeration forms, to reapply on Form 6 as if they were new voters. It asked why voters who had shifted residences could not just disclose details and why deleted voters could not fill enumeration forms belatedly. This is the central design flaw of the SIR as it shifts the burden of enrolment from the state to the elector, including those who have voted before, and treats a mere change of address as ground for deletion. The share of draft deletions recorded as “shifted” or “absent” rose from 55% in Bihar to 72% in States/Union Territories in Phase 3. In Karnataka, about 84 lakh electors were deleted, marked as “shifted” or “absent” during enumeration. But only a net of 8.2 lakh, including new electors, were added during the claims phase, with the final roll being 64.5 lakh short of the projected adult population. Requiring moved voters to re-register as fresh applicants defeats the ECI’s historic mandate of widening the franchise, which was inherent in the 2002-03 intensive revision, where enumerators enrolled shifted voters at their new homes and the Chief Electoral Officer reconciled the old entries.

Justice Bagchi also mentioned that the Bihar judgment was not a “binding precedent” and that the legality of “logical discrepancy” checks, allowed only as an “interim arrangement” in West Bengal, had not been finally adjudicated. No statute or rule provides for judging a voter’s eligibility on the basis of family size or the age gap between voters and parents, which were two of the ECI’s ludicrous and algorithm-driven “logical discrepancy” checks. In West Bengal these checks resulted in massive disenfranchisement and The Hindu’s analysis found that in Delhi, Muslims were disproportionately flagged. But the Court should not merely issue managerial fixes such as extended deadlines or displaying printed lists in blocks, as it has in the past. The final SIR rolls are erroneous as deletions flowed from a flawed design rather than just lapses by the ECI. The dead and duplicate entries that the SIR identified should be removed and newly eligible electors added. Voters wrongly removed from draft rolls must be included again. The larger questions over the Commission’s SIR conduct and how its members are appointed must also be settled.

articles.title: MLC polls: In Maharashtra, ruling Mahayuti gets 2 seats, counting continues for other seats
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: In Maharashtra, the ruling Mahayuti won two seats in the Legislative Council elections. The results for two of the five teachers’ and graduates’ constituencies in the State were officially declared by the Maharashtra Chief Electoral Officer late at night on Wednesday (October 28, 2026). The Bharatiya Janata Party won the Pune Teachers’ constituency, while the Shiv Sena won the Amravati Teachers’ constituency.

Counting was going on for the remaining three seats for the second consecutive day on Wednesday (October 28, 2026). The result for the third seat of the Pune Graduates’ constituency was expected to be declared late at night on Wednesday (October 28, 2026). NCP Sharadchandra Pawar group was leading on the seat till this report went to print.

Meanwhile, the election proved to be a major setback for the ruling NCP, which could not open its account. The dismal trend and the lead taken by NCP SP on the single seat allocated to NCP irked senior leader Praful Patel. “Today’s Vidhan Parishad election results serve as a definitive wake-up call. The time has come for urgent introspection to rebuild trust, realign our priorities, and fix our organisational structure,” he posted on his social media handle X. He had earlier expressed displeasure at the party being denied the Pune seat during the seat distribution talks with allies.

The Teachers’ constituency of Pune had drawn attention in the State for the fight between the Mahayuti partners. The seat was with Congress, which lost in the battle between the two alliance partners. During the seat-sharing talks, the seat was officially given to the BJP, and the Shiv Sena had backed another candidate. On Wednesday (October 28, 2026), BJP candidate Kaustubh Gawade defeated Shiv Sena-backed candidate Sachin Sanap and Congress’ sitting MLC Jayant Asagaonkar. Mr Sanap was an OSD to Sena minister Uday Samant.

Shiv Sena’s Kiran Ramrao Sarnaik won the Amravati Teachers’ constituency for the second time, despite internal strife and rebellions in the Mahayuti. He defeated Congress’ Aditi Pohare and independent candidate Shrikant Deshpande. In Amravati Teachers’ constituency, the BJP and the Shiv Sena have traditionally fought against each other. After the seat was declared to the Shiv Sena in the seat distribution talks, some BJP leaders had rebelled. Three BJP rebels had filed nominations as independents. The party had to expel all three of them. Thereafter, Maharashtra minister and BJP leader Chandrashekhar Bawankule had appealed to Eknath Shinde to act against Sena rebel Shrikant Deshpande. On Wednesday (October 28, 2026), Shiv Sena’s official candidate Mr. Sarnaik, defeated him.

The counting for the three other seats continued for the second day on Wednesday (October 28, 2026). Results were likely to be declared for the third seat of the Pune Graduates’ constituency, where NCP SP’s candidate was leading in the rounds of votes counted till then.

articles.title: Integrated village development programme inaugurated in Nanjangud
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: An Integrated Village Development Programme (IVDP) was launched in Nanjangud by Nestle India on Tuesday in the presence of Nanjangud MLA Darshan Dhruvanarayan.

The programme focuses on strengthening village-level infrastructure and improving quality of life through a range of community-led interventions, including improvements to schools and Anganwadis, installation of Reverse Osmosis (RO) water purification units, pond restoration and other development initiatives, said a statement here.
The IVDP seeks to reaffirm the company’s commitment to supporting inclusive and sustainable community development.
Apart from Mr. Darshan Dhruvanarayan, the programme was attended by Rodrigo Aja Prado, factory manager, Kalale Keshavamurthy, former MLA, and other key government officials.

Speaking on the occasion, Mr. Dhruvanarayan said sustainable rural development requires collective effort and a focus on the needs of local communities. “Initiatives such as Nestlé India’s Integrated Village Development Programme can play an important role in strengthening essential infrastructure and improving access to vital services,” he said.
Factory manager Rodrigo Aja Prado said the company believes that “meaningful community development begins with understanding local needs and working together to address them”.

Through the Integrated Village Development Programme, the company aims to support communities through interventions spanning education, access to safe drinking water and restoration of local resources.
The initiative underscores the importance of collaboration between industry, government and communities in building a more inclusive and sustainable future, a statement from the company added.

articles.title: UNESCO expert committee seeks stronger community participation in Hampi conservation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Four days after the UNESCO experts committee visited the World Heritage Site, Hampi, the experts shared preliminary observations with the senior Tourism Department officials in Vidhana Soudha on October 28.

According to the officials, they have identified areas requiring continued attention, including stronger participation of local communities, enhanced institutional capacity for the Hampi World Heritage Area Management Authority (HWHAMA), continuity in heritage administration and systematic Heritage Impact Assessments for future development projects. A detailed UNESCO expert committee report is expected by mid-December.

UNESCO expert, George Abungu of Kenya described Hampi as an exceptionally significant World Heritage Site and expressed satisfaction with the physical condition of the monuments and the conservation efforts undertaken by the authorities.
He said, “The delegation had come as friends and partners not as investigators, to work with the state and national authorities in identifying strengths, challenges and the way forward.”
Stressing that Hampi is a living community, Prof. Abungu said local people must be active participants in conservation and must also benefit from tourism and heritage development.
Meanwhile, Ichida Shimoda of Japan, another UNESCO expert recommended strengthening HWHAMA with specialised manpower and adequate financial resources.

Development Commissioner and Additional Chief Secretary Uma Mahadevan who was present in this meeting, said, “Hampi’s Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) must be protected without compromise. At the same time, conservation must include the local community. Strong institutions, expert-led planning and administrative continuity are essential for sustainable heritage management.”

articles.title: Manufacturers told to focus on value addition, design-led innovation, tech ownership
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The need for India to move beyond manufacturing scale towards greater domestic value addition, design-led innovation, technology ownership and globally competitive manufacturing ecosystems was emphasised by speakers at a CII conference on advanced manufacturing here on Wednesday.

Addressing the inaugural session, Special Chief Secretary to the State government Navin Mittal highlighted the significant opportunities emerging at the intersection of advanced manufacturing, renewable energy, energy storage, electric mobility, and data centres. “We are literally standing at the threshold of major revolutions in the energy sector,” he said.

Mr. Mittal emphasised the need to strengthen domestic manufacturing across the solar value chain, develop energy-storage capabilities and leverage AI, IoT, digital twins and robotics to improve operational efficiency, CII said in a release.

Chairman of CII Special Taskforce on Advanced Manufacturing Rahul Garg emphasised on the growing role of AI, robotics, Industrial IoT and digital twins in enhancing productivity, product quality and export competitiveness. Founder and Chairman of Cyient B.V.R. Mohan Reddy said India’s next manufacturing phase must focus on technology ownership and design-led innovation rather than production scale alone.

Micron India Managing Director Anand Ramamurthy spoke on the importance of leapfrogging technology, strengthening infrastructure, creating predictable policy frameworks and developing specialised talent to attract and scale advanced manufacturing in India. CII Telangana Chairman M. Goutham Reddy said advanced manufacturing should be sustainability focused.

articles.title: Former MLC moves HC questioning ‘prohibitory list’ of lands, says government targeting BRS leaders
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A writ petition filed by former MLC Elvis Stephenson of BRS seeking suspension of a Government Order placing lands in ‘prohibitory list’ will be heard by a single judge of Telangana High Court.

When the former legislator’s plea came up on Wednesday for hearing initially before it, the bench of Acting Chief Justice P. Sam Koshy and Justice Suddala Chalapathi Rao directed the Registry to place the same before a single judge. The GO Ms. No. 341 issued by the State government on this September 23 was challenged by the petitioner, contending that it aimed at selectively targetting BRS leaders.

According to the petitioner, the GO was being used by the present government to target its political rivals and placed lands of 16 BRS leaders in the prohibitory list. The targetted leaders included former Chief Minister K. Chandrasekhara Rao, K.T. Rama Rao, M. Hanumantha Rao (father-in-law of T. Harish Rao), G. Jagadishwar Reddy, Pilot Rohit Reddy, Palla Rajeshwar Reddy Joginapally Ravinder Rao, J. Sowmya and others, the petitioner stated.

The former MLC stated in the plea that he was the complainant in the ‘çash for vote’ case involving present Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy. He claimed that Revanth Reddy, who was MLA in 2015 from Telugu Desam Party, offered a bribe of ₹ 50 lakh to him to vote in MLC election as he was nominated MLC from BRS then. The Anti-Corruption Bureau officials registered a case and arrested Mr. Revanth Reddy then, he explained.

The petitioner contended that Mr. Revanth Reddy was the first accused in the case which was pending for adjudication before the Supreme Court now. Mr. Reddy had targetted BRS leaders since he was arrested in the cash for vote case, the petitioner contended.

articles.title: Intensify inspection to stop child labour: ADC
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Mysuru district administration has instructed officials to intensify inspection and initiate legal action against those employing children in the district.

While conducting the quarterly review meeting of the district level executive and task force committee of the District Child Labour Project Society on Tuesday, Additional Deputy Commissioner (ADC) R. Aishwarya directed officials to take immediate action to prevent children from selling pens, pencils, balloons and other items at the Dasara Exhibition Ground.
Employing children below the age of 18 in stalls and shops at the Dasara Exhibition is strictly prohibited, said ADC.

With Deepavali approaching, ADC instructed officials to maintain strict vigilance and create awareness among owners of firecracker manufacturing units and sales outlets against the employment of those below 18 years, according to a press release.

She said that officials who had been notified as inspector under Section 16 and 17 of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, must conduct minimum 15 inspections every month in their hobli without fail.

The ADC had directed Tahashildars to conduct a regular meeting of taluk-level child labour eradication and rehabilitation committees. She also instructed officials to conduct awareness programmes about Child Labour Act in schools and public places with the co-ordination of government department.

articles.title: Vedanta Group eyeing $20 billion profits over next two years: Chairman Anil Agarwal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Vedanta Group is targeting revenue of $50 billion and profits of $20 billion over the next two years, founder and chairman Anil Agarwal said at an industry event in Kolkata.
“This year we would be making $30 billion revenue and $11 billion in profits. In two years, we would scale our revenues to $50 billion with $20 billion in profits,” he said.
The privately-owned diversified commodities producer has interests spanning aluminium, zinc, oil and gas, power, iron and steel, copper and other critical minerals.

Separately, its recently listed Vedanta Aluminium reported more than a doubling of net profit year-on-year to ₹6,187 crore for the quarter ended September. Revenue rose 41% to ₹22,066 crore during the period.
The company increased aluminium production by 5% year-on-year to 649 kilotonnes (KT). Production of value-added aluminium products rose 31% to 432 KT, while alumina output climbed 37% to 895 KT.

Vedanta Aluminium also reduced its net debt by ₹3,090 crore during the quarter compared with the preceding quarter, signalling an improvement in its debt position alongside higher production and earnings.

articles.title: The way out of the dangerous trap
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: India, celebrated as the world’s fastest-growing economy, has become the world’s fourth-largest economy, and is expected to be the next engine of global growth. Yet beneath these numbers lies a grim reality: India is drifting toward the middle-income trap, in which countries exhaust their gains from cheap labour and rapid catch-up and fail to transition to an innovation-driven, productivity-based economy. Weak job creation, stagnant wages, sluggish private investment, and low productivity are reinforcing one another, threatening to stall the country’s rise before it reaches high-income status. Many countries in the Global South are caught in this trap. India’s structural crisis is unique and more serious than not just a consequence of wars in West Asia disturbing its supply chain or premature automation from AI.

The signs of distress are visible in the youth protests across the country. Private investment remains sluggish, wage growth is stagnant, and household consumption is weak. Manufacturing has failed to generate enough jobs, while post-pandemic recovery has favoured large corporations and the digital economy, leaving the informal sector barely touched. Jobless growth emerges because productivity gains stay concentrated in narrow, capital- and skill-intensive enclaves that create little employment. This simultaneous rise of rising inequality and low productivity is a dangerous trap.

Economists are typically divided in explaining this trap. Those trained in pro-market orthodoxy argue India needs another set of market reforms — no less than what occurred during the 1991 moment — more labour flexibility, agricultural reform, deregulation, and infrastructure investment. Those on the left and typically in the Keynesian mould argue that the economy suffers from weak aggregate demand and needs more public spending, redistribution and social protection. Both arguments hold a kernel of truth, but miss the larger point: India’s current situation stems not only from supply and demand constraints but from institutions shaped by social norms, which decide both how markets set incentives and prices, and how the State allocates resources and provides public goods.

It is no surprise, then, that both the State and the market operate suboptimally. Private capital, more freer from regulation than ever, does not do well on productivity and innovation. Its competitiveness comes from cutting costs rather than innovating. It couldn’t even absorb knowledge that comes with FDI. It couldn’t increase productivity that results from both inter-sectoral movements and innovation within sectors either. On the other hand, capital is heavily subsidised, lowering its relative price vis-à-vis labour in a labour-surplus economy. India’s innovation is skewed, with R&D spending at a paltry 0.65% of GDP, while technology adoption remains weak and far from spontaneous. Despite the government’s growing size, India’s capacity to intervene — even to provide basic services like health centres or schooling — remains among the lowest anywhere.

The Left–Right debate focuses on the size and quality of government expenditure, but the problem lies elsewhere. The same social norms that shape resource allocation also drive its inefficient use. For instance, India has historically underfunded mass education while subsidising higher education for elites, tilting spending toward the privileged. That same elite bias later drove the service-sector-heavy growth of post-reform India, letting upper castes monopolise better occupations while relegating low-productivity work to others.

India’s social norms are distinctive: they decide how State and market function while producing durable inequality and legitimising it. Having long undermined mass education, India’s vocational training system remains poorly managed and chronically underfunded. Fewer than 3% of the workforce has any formal vocational education. Of roughly 14,000 ITIs offering about 25 lakh seats, actual intake is only about 48%, and even among graduates, the employment rate is just 63% — far below the 90%-plus seen in many other countries.

Societies set up institutions based on their interests and norms. Economists often take self-interest as central to economic motives. Yet social norms determine the kind of institutions that take shape, which in turn decide how individual efforts are channelised into productive activities. These institutions work as the taproot of entrepreneurial success. As this year’s Nobel Prize winner Joel Mokyr has argued, modern growth depends on the accumulation and diffusion of “useful knowledge,” the practical skills that enable societies to innovate, adapt and raise productivity.

For Mokyr, sustained growth rests on the coevolution of science, technology and the spread of useful knowledge, something that failed to take strong root in India. India has historically privileged abstract education over vocational and technical knowledge. University degrees command prestige while technical courses training electricians, welders, machinists and carpenters do not. This hierarchy is not accidental. It reflects centuries of caste-based occupational stratification, where manual and artisanal work has been systematically undervalued despite its indispensable role in industrial development.

The result is a chronic shortage of skilled manufacturing workers even as millions of educated young Indians struggle to find decent jobs. Ironically, India’s Chief Economic Adviser, V Anantha Nageswaran, recently urged the youth to pursue trades such as welding and plumbing instead of chasing software jobs or MBAs.

But it won’t happen unless India changes its social valuation of skills. Take the marriage market: some skills and occupations carry a premium over others. These social valuations shape educational choices, occupational aspirations and ultimately the allocation of labour.

Data show a persistent and steady decline in the labour intensity of production technology across sectors. Even in traditionally labour-intensive sectors, the trend is likely to accelerate with the advent of AI. India therefore needs to recalibrate not just production and distribution, but also their valuation. Without changing the cultural valuation of skills and the way production itself is organised. India may fall into a low-income, low-productivity trap.

Countries that escaped the middle-income trap — from South Korea to China — did not simply build factories but built institutions capable of creating and diffusing useful knowledge across domains. China’s interventions in education and health laid the foundation for its later productive capacity. Its early state-led industrialisation was accompanied by massive investments in technical education, local manufacturing capability and technological learning. By contrast, countries such as Brazil, Argentina, Thailand and the Philippines, which failed to build or sustain such institutions, became stuck in the middle-income trap. Like India, large sections of their populations remain dependent on public transfers and handouts to secure the basic requirements of a prosperous existence.

articles.title: The gap in manufacturing sector GVA
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Early this year, the National Statistical Office (NSO) released the new series of the National Accounts Statistics (NAS). It shows that the manufacturing sector’s gross value added (GVA) is ₹38.6 lakh crore (₹38.6 trillion), constituting 14.7 per cent of GDP (gross domestic product) for the year 2023-24 at current prices. How reliable is the official estimate? This article investigates.

The manufacturing sector has two parts: One comprises all registered factories employing 10+/20+ workers with/without power, including registered companies (defined as the organised/formal sector). The other comprises unincorporated/ informal/ household units consisting of small factories/workshops falling outside the corporate/factory sector. The Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) reports the production accounts of the factory sector, while the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) covers the informal sector. The combined output (GVA) of the factory and unincorporated sectors almost completely represents total manufacturing output.

For 2023-24, the sum of the GVA of units covered by the ASI and ASUSE is ₹27.4 lakh crore (the Alternative Estimate or, AE). The official figure, as per the NAS, is ₹38.6 lakh crore. It is higher than the AE by a whopping 40.9 per cent. Let’s call this the GAP. What could account for it?

While minor variations between the two estimates is understandable due to methodological or definitional issues, such a substantial GAP between the two estimates using official data sources surely raises many questions.

What are the data sources used for estimating the official GVA? For the unincorporated sector, it is ASUSE – the same as what we have used to estimate the AE. Hence, it cannot account for the GAP noted above. Moreover, the unincorporated sector’s share in total manufacturing GVA is a mere 13.9 per cent.

Hence, the reason for the GAP must lie in the estimation of organised manufacturing output. The NAS uses company balance-sheet data sourced from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ database (MCA-21), compiled using the annual statutory filings by registered companies. This practice of using the MCA data began with the previous NAS revision (base year 2011-12), partially replacing the ASI. The procedure has continued in the latest revision, with minor modifications.

A standard way to validate the GVA is to use employment data to estimate the sector’s potential output by applying appropriate “technical ratios” drawn from the ASI and ASUSE datasets. The official Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for 2023-24, estimated that the manufacturing sector employed 697.5 lakh workers.

However, as per the ASI and ASUSE datasets, only 532.9 lakh workers were employed to produce the official GVA. Thus, quite possibly, the contribution of the remaining 164.6 lakh “residual workers” — 697.5 minus 532.9 — may account for the GAP in the GVA reported above.

The definitions of employment in the three surveys are not the same, and their data collection methods differ. However, for a validation exercise, the PLFS estimates provide a useful reference point. Official agencies also use similar methods.

Some of this GAP is contributed by the residual 2,72,534 MCA companies, not covered in the 78,618 “private companies” captured in the ASI data. A majority of the residual companies are likely to be to non-factory private companies. The left over residual workers are likely to belong to the unincorporated sector not covered in ASUSE survey because of their small size.

Then, applying the “technical ratios” of the appropriate segments of manufacturing as derived from unit-wise ASI and ASUSE data, the potential GVA of the residual workers is estimated to be ₹3.6 lakh crore.
Then adding the potential GVA to the AE of ₹27.4 lakh crore reported earlier, the likely/potential overall manufacturing GVA could be ₹31.0 lakh crore.

articles.title: India and Mexico sign Terms of Reference for preferential trade agreement negotiations to begin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: India and Mexico on Wednesday signed the Terms of Reference (ToR) to start negotiations on a trade deal between the two countries, the government announced following the signing in Mexico.

The signing of the ToR follows an understanding reached between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum during their meeting on the sidelines of the G7 Summit in Canada in June 2025.

“Mexico and India take an important step towards strengthening their economic and trade relations with the signing of the Terms of Reference for negotiations on a Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA), which establish the framework, scope, modalities and roadmap for negotiations aimed at creating new economic opportunities for both countries,” the government said in a release.

During the signing, the Indian side was represented by Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal, who held discussions with Mexico’s Undersecretary of Foreign Trade Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez Romano, who participated on behalf of Secretary of Economy Marcelo Ebrard Casaubon.

“The Terms of Reference cover key negotiating areas, including market access for goods, rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, dispute settlement, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade and trade remedies,” the release said.

“With its strong linkages to global value chains, Mexico is an important market for Indian exporters and investors,” it added. “Sectors with significant potential for cooperation include automotive, chemicals, electronics, pharmaceuticals, agri-food, energy, critical minerals, medical devices and advanced manufacturing, among others.”
Mr. Agrawal and Mr. Romano also discussed the possibility of organising a Mexican business mission to India during the first quarter of 2027.

“The proposed mission would facilitate business-to-business meetings, help identify commercial opportunities and strengthen commercial ties between the productive sectors of the two countries,” the government said.

articles.title: On the question of KIIFB’s future
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: In July, Keralam’s newly elected UDF government set up an expert panel to review the functioning of Kerala Infrastructure Investment Fund Board (KIIFB). The panel, headed by a former civil servant, was tasked with recommending measures to restructure KIIFB and strengthen the government’s institutional capabilities, among other things. The committee has recently submitted its report, which has been tabled in the State Assembly.

Apparently critical of KIIFB’s functioning, the committee has recommended winding it up; absorbing its functions and capabilities into the State government, news reports say. The principal reason for the panel’s recommendation is that with the clubbing of KIIFB’s borrowing function with the State budget, the special purpose vehicle (SPV) has lost its primary purpose.

KIIFB, restructured by the LDF government, reportedly boosted the State’s infrastructure investment by raising extra-budgetary resources, including securing soft loans known as “Masala Bonds” from international agencies after the disastrous floods of 2019. However, the SPV’s functioning and financial performance have remained contentious. The comptroller and auditor general’s (CAG) strictures against KIIFB have become a convenient beating stick for the Centre and the Opposition parties in the State. Leftist critics have branded it as the arm of “the Left Managerial State” for promoting controversial projects, bypassing legislative approvals. In the fog of the debate, KIIFB’s original purpose and economic principles underlying it seem to have been lost sight of. We seek to explain them, intending to shed some light on the contentious issue.

Though Keralam has sound traditional transport infrastructure such as road network and rail connectivity, it lags behind in modern facilities, such as high-speed railways or highways, especially when compared to the neighbouring States. Keralam reportedly spends a mere 1.5 per cent of the Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) on infrastructure. This was so in spite of Keralam’s own-tax revenue to GSDP ratio being among the highest among major States, as per the RBI data.

KIIFB was set up in 1999 and underwent a major restructuring in 2016; the institution’s record in expanding public goods is apparently well acknowledged. However, its functioning raised many queries. The CAG found that the SPV’s finances flouted its procedural audits, which became a sticking point between the Centre and the State. Moreover, as KIIFB functioned outside the purview of the State budget, without generating financial profits from its lending, its borrowings being serviced out of the State’s revenue became the heart of the contention.

In the good/bad old days of “planning”, State finances broadly followed the “gap-filling” approach; meaning the Centre made up the difference between a State’s projected revenue growth and its “developmental needs” as per the State plans. It was a negotiated process, part financial and part political. Evidence shows that richer and politically influential States got the lion’s share of the divisible pool of the plan resources.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBM) 2003 changed that by seemingly imposing a “hard budget constraint”, with the fiscal deficit capped at 3 per cent of GSDP. The RBI now monitors the size of the State debt. The coupon (interest) rate of the State loans depends on the State’s debt sustainability measures. The hard budget constraint has reportedly improved State finances, or at a minimum, made them transparent.

However, most States have devised a variety of means for securing extra-budgetary resources, or off-budget borrowings (OBBs) – as evident from the RBI’s compilation of State finances. The CAG, tracking OBBs, finds that there is a bewildering variety of them. And the actual OBBs are far higher than what it is able to count, as per its own findings. In other words, ensuring fiscal discipline seems like a cat-and-mouse game between the Centre and States. Incidentally, Keralam is not among the worst offenders.

Globally, a variety of financial institutions and fiscal arrangements have existed outside of the budgetary process. Numerous kinds of para-statal organisations are a feature – not a bug – of the fiscal landscape, especially among fast-growing Asian economies. China, for instance, has a bewildering variety of financial arrangements that enable provinces to draw resources from the national development banks to sustain employment at the local level, augment production and exports and ensure political stability. No wonder, China’s public debt to GDP ratio is nearly 300 per cent – though most of it domestic.

Then, realistically, what should be the rules for managing extra-budgetary resources and institutions for Keralam? Simply speaking, if extra-budgetary resources are productively used and they comply with the government expenditure principles, having such off-budget institutions/borrowings may not be undesirable. This follows the Domar rule: so long as the output growth rate exceeds the interest rate on such loans (either at current or at constant prices), they are being used productively. Since such investments have a public good character, individual projects may not be yielding adequate revenue or covering the full costs. However, if in the aggregate they contribute to growth in state output (GSDP) and follow the Domar rule, then such investments are in principle viable.

However, if the State-level SPVs borrow from external sources for social purposes or green financing, which usually have lower interest rates for longer maturities, they need to be assessed differently, as they involve exchange rate risk. Given Keralam’s fragile ecology and need for substantial low-cost resources for protecting it, external borrowing for such purposes by creating SPVs may be desirable, as KIIFB reportedly proved to be after the floods in 2019. The expert committee’s recommendation to dissolve KIIFB is the easier part. In the present political milieu, efforts to boost public investments to catch up with the neighbouring States are a harder job – with the Centre strictly monitoring Keralam. The State will have to devise newer and administratively innovative means to tap OBBs, as most States do. The task is primarily a political one.

articles.title: What the new E100 vehicle rules mean | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The story so far: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has amended the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 , to permit the use of ethanol-based fuels containing up to 100% ethanol (E100) in vehicles. The move paves the way for flex-fuel vehicles, which can run on petrol, ethanol blends of varying proportions, or pure ethanol.
The amendments modify Rule 115, which deals with emission standards and related requirements for motor vehicles, and Rule 115E, which contains additional provisions relating to emission testing.

One of the key changes is the inclusion of E100, or fuel comprising 100% ethanol, alongside E85 in several tables under Rule 115. E85 is a fuel containing up to 85% ethanol, while E100 consists entirely of ethanol, subject to applicable fuel specifications.
The amendments include an explanatory note stating that E85 or E100 may be used only in flex-fuel vehicles designed by original equipment manufacturers.

No. In a press statement, the Ministry sought to allay concerns among motorists, clarifying that a vehicle’s compatibility with E10 or E20 does not establish its suitability for E85. The notification does not require owners of existing vehicles to switch to E85 or modify their vehicles, either now or in the future.

Motorists should check the fuel-compatibility sticker on their vehicle and follow the manufacturer’s guidance in the owner’s manual when choosing fuel at a filling station, the Ministry statement added.

The amendments are expected to facilitate homologation, the official certification process through which authorised agencies, such as the Automotive Research Association of India, verify that vehicles and components comply with technical, safety and environmental standards before they can be approved for sale or use on public roads.
This will help secure type approvals for E100-powered vehicles, supporting their rollout and wider consumer adoption.
Corrections have also been incorporated into fuel classifications, including a reference to gasoline blended with 20% ethanol, or E20, in place of an earlier notation referring to E10.

India achieved its 20% ethanol-blending (E20) target in 2025 , five years ahead of the original 2030 deadline set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018. From April 2026, all Bharat Stage-VI (BS-VI) vehicles are required to fully meet E20 emission standards, and all petrol sold across India is mandated to contain 20% ethanol (E20). The policy focus is now widening beyond E20: the government has enabled the regulatory pathway for E85 and E100 vehicles, though these fuels will require compatible flex-fuel vehicles and dedicated dispensing infrastructure.

The main concern is vehicle compatibility. Owners of older or non-E20-compliant vehicles question whether E20 could damage components, raise maintenance costs, or leave them without access to lower-ethanol petrol.

Consumers also question E20’s effect on fuel economy. Ethanol has a lower energy density than petrol; while the government estimates a 5% decline in mileage, some consumers say the loss is greater. Dealers, meanwhile, warn that ethanol’s affinity for water could raise contamination risks during the monsoon, strengthening the case for separate storage and dispensing systems for higher blends. These concerns have prompted calls for a transparent assessment.

articles.title: Iran warns of 'devastating' economic fallout from any new Israeli attack
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Iran on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) warned of a devastating economic impact from any new Israeli-led attack, as the votes were counted in an Israeli election that could determine the future of the regional war.
Under Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has vowed to topple Iran's government, the two countries have directly fought a war for the first time in their history after decades of enmity.

Tuesday's (October 27) pivotal election gave Israelis a chance to offer a verdict on Netanyahu's right-wing government, amid mounting U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran following their launch of the war in February.

"Devastating impact on int'l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Persian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X, referring to recent discussions at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow.

Since the war erupted, it has severely disrupted energy shipments from Gulf countries after Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel.
Iran has restricted passage and regularly attacks vessels that attempt to cross without its authorisation.
In retaliation, the United States has been maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports, seeking to squeeze the country's economy.

On Wednesday (October 28), the Wall Street Journal reported that Washington had told several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible "short, intense military campaign" against Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
But the newspaper, citing people briefed on the conversations, said President Donald Trump had not made a final decision.
Mr. Netanyahu, vying to form a coalition government after the closely contested polls, has said Israel has an opportunity to eliminate the "existential threat" posed by Iran.
His main electoral rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, has warned Israel's security top brass that they must serve the national interests and not the political needs of Mr. Netanyahu.
"Mr. Netanyahu, don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.

articles.title: News Analysis | What has driven the high Arab turnout in Israel’s elections?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Israel’s October 27 legislative elections recorded a massive voter turnout of 77.7%, the highest since 1999. The country’s Arab citizens, who turned up in massive numbers to vote, remained one of the main factors, contributing to the surge.

While the official figures for voter turnout among Israeli Arabs are yet to be released by the Central Elections Committee, exit polls recorded by Channel 12 estimate Arab voter turnout to be nearly 80%. This implies that the voter turnout among Arab citizens in Israel would be the highest in at least a decade.

While Arabs account for about 21% of Israel’s population, the parties representing them have never held more than 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset. Their turnout in the elections has also been relatively low, with about 40% of eligible Arab adults abstaining from voting in most Knesset elections over the past two decades.

“In the previous elections, I think the low voter turnout was a result of disappointment mainly from Arab parties themselves. We know that approximately 10% of Arab citizens boycott Knesset elections for ideological reasons, but the majority are reluctant to take part in this political game because of the conduct of their parties,” said Arik Rudnitzky, from the Israel Democracy Institute in Jerusalem.

This trend was defied in the latest election. “I believe the number one motivator specifically in these elections is fear. Fear of another term of the Netanyahu government or a right-wing government because Arab citizens have had enough in the past four years,” Mr. Rudnitzky told The Hindu.

This surge was used by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition to mobilise right-wing voters. Mr. Netanyahu, on his X, called on his supporters to vote for Likud and described the situation as a “matter of life and death”.
His posts tried to mobilise voters by calling the situation “a war at home.” This attempt was criticised by Arab parties for being racist and for inciting hatred.

A survey by the Israel Democracy Institute published in September revealed that a party’s position regarding foreign affairs and security, followed by the economy and high cost of living, were the two most influential factors determining the support of Jewish Israelis.
In contrast, more than half of the surveyed Arabs felt that the party’s position regarding crime in Arab society was one of the most important factors determining their vote.

A large voter turnout among Israeli Arabs is expected to benefit the Arab parties, thereby improving the chances of Arab representation in the Knesset committees and better policies or support for them. This is evident in the exit polls and latest numbers which have put Arab parties leading in at least 17 seats in the Knesset

However, it is also true that not all Arab citizens support Arab parties. “In general, approximately 15% of the Arab or Arab citizens support non-Arab parties, Jewish parties. Most of them support centrist parties. Also the Democrats headed by Yair Golan enjoy relative significant support in the Arab sector,” said Mr. Rudnitzky.

Latest numbers also show that neither the Netanyahu-bloc nor the Opposition coalition is set to secure a clear majority, meaning that Arab parties could hold the key as to who forms the government this time.

articles.title: Netanyahu bloc leads Israel vote, falls short of majority
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Results from Israel’s hard-fought election pointed on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) to no clear winner as a leader of the Arab minority appealed to a hesitant opposition to join forces to end the divisive reign of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

With more than three quarters of the vote counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc was slightly ahead but short of a majority in Tuesday’s (October 27, 2026) election, the first since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, which has led Israel to wage war on Gaza and across the region.

Both Mr. Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief leading a broad opposition bloc, vowed that they would seek to form the next government. But neither looks set to reach the 61-seat threshold for a majority. With 77% of ballots counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc had 54 of the 120 seats in Parliament and Mr. Eisenkot’s opposition had 49.
The results could still change but one place of clear gains was among Israeli Arab lists which were set to jump to 17 seats.

Voters from the Arab community, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after Israel’s creation and who make up around 20% of the population, have been enraged by the Netanyahu government’s ultra-nationalist Jewish vision for the country and the Palestinian territories.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the leftist Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership, and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”.
“It’s either the continuation of racism, the continuation of exclusion and the continuation of supremacy, or a genuine Jewish-Arab partnership,” he said.

Mr. Eisenkot has resisted allying with Arab parties. Mr. Netanyahu during the campaign relentlessly attacked the opposition by saying it would put Arabs in power, running on the slogan: “Either the Right or Palestine.”
Yair Golan, the head of Israel’s main left-wing party and a member of Mr. Eisenkot’s camp, became the first member of the opposition camp to call for an alliance with Arab parties.
But Mr. Eisenkot’s camp also includes right-wingers who share many of Netanyahu’s hawkish views and have adamantly rejected working with Arab lawmakers.

articles.title: Trump says Putin-Zelensky meeting to be set up 'very soon'
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky would be set up "very soon."
The announcement came as Trump's administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.
"There'll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made," Mr. Trump told reporters.
Mr. Zelensky said on Sunday that a trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks.
The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November.
Mr. Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Mr. Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Mr. Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours — but over a year of U.S.-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.
In recent days, Mr. Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Mr. Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.

articles.title: At least 68 dead after two trains collide in Spain’s Toledo Province
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed at least 68 people and injured scores more on Wednesday (October 28, 2026), with the toll likely to rise, authorities said, in one of Europe’s deadliest such disasters this century.

The second such accident to strike Spain in 2026 will raise fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, with the Transport Minister speaking of an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the collision.

AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another and some carriages lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment.
Dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site during a frantic search for survivors, while several black vans arrived from a funeral parlour.
Castilla-La Mancha’s leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene that 68 people had died, raising an earlier toll of 64 and having already warned of more victims being found.
A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha regional government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured. Of them, 58 had been taken to hospital, with 15 in a critical condition.

State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.

People check an information screen displaying a message that the high-speed train line between Madrid and Andalucia has been interrupted following the collision of two high-speed trains between the towns of Mora and Orgaz at Atocha train station in Madrid, Spain, on October 28, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters
Pablo Mejia, 42, with blood staining his grey jumper, told AFP that he had miraculously survived after changing his seat, as he awaited a transfer to the southern city of Seville.
He recounted “a very strong hit. It lasted a long time until it stopped, lots of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos”.
A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz who lives in the village of Urda close to the site of the accident, around 130km south of Madrid, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.
Ortiz, 49, described a “horrific, horrible” scene that “smelled of an accident, of metal”.

articles.title: Afghan-Pakistan border clash kills one, injures five
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A clash on the restive border between Afghanistan and Pakistan killed one person and injured five, Pakistan officials said Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
The countries went to war earlier this year and, with no permanent resolution reached on security issues, there have been sporadic attacks since a March truce.
Pakistan accuses Afghanistan of harbouring militants responsible for deadly attacks on its territory, an allegation the Taliban government in Afghanistan denies.

Homes and shops were targeted in the market town of Angoor Adda during the cross-border fire from Afghanistan, according to the office of the deputy commissioner in Pakistan's South Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province.
It blamed the "unprovoked" attack on Afghanistan's Taliban authorities.
A senior administrative official in South Waziristan, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP the casualties were caused by mortar fire from Afghanistan.
Pakistani forces responded with a "brief operation targeting the Afghan side with artillery fire", targeting an Afghan checkpoint, the official said.
They said they could not confirm any casualties on the Afghan side of the border.
A security official in Angoor Adda also confirmed the attack.
The governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province, Faisal Karim Kundi, condemned the "unprovoked and blatant aggression by the Afghan Taliban regime against civilian homes".
Hundreds of civilians have been killed in fighting between the two countries since October last year, according to figures from the United Nations' mission in Afghanistan.
